source.title: Analyzing Visual Aircraft Representations with Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders to analyze vision-model representations, with neuron polysemanticity discussed as motivation, but it does not measure individual neurons or test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports qualitative interpretations and statistics for eight SAE latent features, plus ablations of those features and associated image regions. These results concern SAE features, not individual neurons, so they do not test the listed versions. The input-space and feature-space ablations test prediction relevance, not whether neurons have coherent or mixed meanings.
record.test_reason: The study trains an SAE on ConvNeXt-Tiny final-stage activations and analyzes eight selected SAE latents. It never measures individual neurons or channels. Neuron polysemanticity appears only as background motivation in Related Work (2.3). The 'polysemanticity' the authors report concerns SAE features, not neurons, so no claim version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAE features are partially interpretable and point to prediction-relevant regions: expanded target blurring flips 22% of predictions versus 4.5% for random blurring. However, single-feature suppression barely changes outputs and flips none, so evidence is distributed and the features are polysemantic and context-dependent.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains an SAE on spatial activations from one fine-tuned ConvNeXt-Tiny aircraft classifier and analyzes selected latent features; it does not use the original neuron-level analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports stronger input-space effects for expanded 3 × 3 target-region blurring than for single-patch blurring, while local feature suppression has almost no effect and global feature suppression has modest effects.

fits_no_version.finding: Eight manually selected SAE latents in the final stage of a fine-tuned ConvNeXt-Tiny each have a dominant aircraft-part theme. They also activate on nearby or other regions, and the authors call them not perfectly monosemantic. This is qualitative, based on top-50 patches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents trained on vision-classifier activations can themselves be partially polysemantic (part-context mixtures), not cleanly monosemantic.

record.problems: Only one architecture, dataset, and activation layer are studied. Qualitative interpretations rely on manual inspection, and ablations cover only eight manually selected SAE features. The feature-level results do not establish how individual neurons behave.
record.rows_left_out: Input-space and feature-space ablation results in Tables 2–7 were left out because they measure prediction effects of perturbing regions or SAE features, not whether individual neurons have coherent or mixed meanings.

untested.parts: Individual ConvNeXt channels/neurons are never inspected; only SAE latents are.
Superposition is cited as background only; there is no test of capacity or sparsity causes.
One architecture is studied, with no comparison of activation functions or regularization for neuron polysemanticity.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
There is no analysis of how the activation range or explanation scoring affects neuron polysemanticity. Only the top-50 patches of SAE latents are inspected.

record.verdict_notes: The study's use of 'polysemantic' refers to SAE latents, not neurons, so it should not be counted as evidence for V1 despite being a vision model. Leaving the ablation tables out of the rows is appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: Individual neurons in image classifiers responding to several unrelated inputs.
Transformer language-model MLP neurons and variation by layer.
Whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure from initialization, regularization, or training noise.
Comparisons of neuron polysemanticity across activations, architectures, or regularization, and performance costs.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons resolve to shared features or related jobs when examined with better tools.
How neuron polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation scoring.
